title: Plans & the future
goal: Talk about plans, intentions and wishes using the future tense, 'want to', 'be about to' and 'I intend to'.
intro:
The Sindhi future is built from the verb stem + **-nd-** + an ending for person and gender: **ويندس** (vendus) 'I'll go', **ايندو** (endo) 'he'll come', **ڪنداسين** (kandāsīṃ) 'we'll do'. You already met the third-person forms in the weather unit.

Talking about the future in Sindh often comes with **انشاءالله** (inshāallāh, 'God willing') — used by Muslims and many others simply as 'hopefully'.

vocab.note: m. Also پروگرام progrāmu (very common: 'what's the programme?').
m. منهنجو ارادو آهي ته … = I intend to …
مان وڃڻ چاهيان ٿو = I want to go.
m. Shrines hold annual ميلا with music and stalls.

phrases.native: سڀاڻي توهان جو ڇا پروگرام آهي؟
phrases.roman: subhāṇe tavhāṃ jo chhā progrāmu āhe?
phrases.en: What are your plans for tomorrow?
I'll go to Sukkur next month. (man)
We'll go to the village for Eid.

phrases.native: مان ڪوشش ڪندس، پر پڪ ناهي.
phrases.roman: māṃ koshisha kandus, para paka nāhe.
phrases.en: I'll try, but I'm not sure. (man)

phrases.native: مان سنڌي چڱيءَ طرح سکڻ چاهيان ٿي.
phrases.roman: māṃ sindhī chaṅgīa tarha sikhaṇu chāhyāṃ thī.
phrases.en: I want to learn Sindhi properly. (woman)

phrases.native: منهنجو ارادو آهي ته ڀٽ شاهه جو ميلو ڏسان.
phrases.roman: munhinjo irādo āhe ta bhiṭ shāh jo melo ɗisāṃ.
phrases.en: I intend to see the fair at Bhit Shah.
Next week we'll have a meal together.
See you soon! (lit. we'll meet soon)

grammar.title: The future tense
grammar.body:
The future is **stem + -nd- + ending**. The endings agree in person, gender and number. Here is وڃڻ (future stem وين- ven-):

مان ويندس vendus (m) / وينديس vendīs (f) — I will go
تون ويندين vendeṃ (m) / vendīṃ (f) — you (intimate) will go
هو ويندو vendo / هوءَ ويندي vendī — he / she will go
اسين وينداسين vendāsīṃ — we will go
توهان ويندؤ vendau (m) / وينديون vendyūṃ (f) — you (polite) will go
هو ويندا vendā (m) / وينديون vendyūṃ (f) — they will go

Regular verbs just add the endings to the stem (with a linking -a- after a consonant): ڏسڻ → ڏسندس ɗisandus, لکڻ → لکندس likhandus, رهڻ → رهندو rahando. After a vowel: کائڻ → کائيندس khāīndus, ڳالهائڻ → ڳالهائيندس.

Irregular futures: **ڪرڻ → ڪندس** kandus · **اچڻ → ايندس** endus · **وڃڻ → ويندس** vendus · **ڏيڻ → ڏيندس** ɗīndus · **هجڻ (to be) → هوندس** hundus · **ٿيڻ → ٿيندو** thīndo.

The negative uses **نه** (or ڪونه, emphatic): مان نه ويندس 'I won't go', مان ڪونه ايندس 'I'm not coming'.

examples.native: مان سڀاڻي توهان کي فون ڪندس.
examples.roman: māṃ subhāṇe tavhāṃ khe fon kandus.

examples.native: ماروي آچر تي ڪراچيءَ کان ايندي.
examples.roman: Mārvī āchara te karāchīa khāṃ endī.
examples.en: Marvi will come from Karachi on Sunday.

examples.native: مان اڄ رات ڪونه سمهندس — ڪم گهڻو آهي.
examples.roman: māṃ aʄu rāti kona sumhandus — kamu ghaṇo āhe.
examples.en: I won't sleep tonight — there's a lot of work.

grammar.title: Wanting, intending and 'about to'
grammar.body:
**Want to + verb**: infinitive + **چاهڻ** (present): مان سکڻ چاهيان ٿو 'I want to learn'. To want **someone else** to do something, use **ته** + the subjunctive (the present form without ٿو): مان چاهيان ٿو ته تون اچين 'I want you to come'.

**Intention**: منهنجو ارادو آهي ته … 'my intention is that …', or مان سوچيان ٿو ته … 'I'm thinking of …'.

**About to / going to (very soon)**: oblique infinitive + **وارو** (agreeing) + آهي: مان وڃڻ وارو آهيان 'I'm about to go' (m), بس نڪرڻ واري آهي 'the bus is about to leave' (f).

**Shall we …?** uses the subjunctive 1st plural: هلون؟ 'shall we go?', چانهه پيئون؟ 'shall we have tea?'.

examples.en: I want to become a doctor. (girl)

examples.native: امان چاهي ٿي ته اسين عيد تي گهر اچون.
examples.roman: amāṃ chāhe thī ta asīṃ ʿīda te ghara achūṃ.
examples.en: Mum wants us to come home for Eid.
The film is about to start.

examples.native: مان سوچيان ٿو ته نئين ڪار وٺان.
examples.roman: māṃ sochyāṃ tho ta naīṃ kāra vaṭhāṃ.
examples.en: I'm thinking of buying a new car. (man)
Shall we go? It's getting late.

dialogue.title: Plans for Cheti Chand
dialogue.setting: Kavita, visiting relatives in Hyderabad, talks with her friend Sanam about the coming holiday.

lines.speaker: Sanam
lines.native: ڪويتا، ايندڙ هفتي جو ڇا پروگرام آهي؟
lines.roman: Kavitā, endaṛa hafte jo chhā progrāmu āhe?
lines.en: Kavita, what are your plans for next week?

lines.speaker: Kavita
lines.native: چيٽي چنڊ آهي! اسين سڀ ماسيءَ جي گهر گڏ ٿينداسين.
lines.roman: cheṭī chanḍu āhe! asīṃ sabhu māsīa je ghara gaɗu thīndāsīṃ.
lines.en: It's Cheti Chand! We'll all gather at my aunt's house.

lines.speaker: Kavita
lines.native: صبح جو مندر وينداسين، پوءِ درياهه تي بهراڻو کڻي وينداسين.
lines.roman: subuh jo mandira vendāsīṃ, poi daryāha te baharāṇo khaṇī vendāsīṃ.
lines.en: In the morning we'll go to the temple, then we'll carry the bahrano offering to the river.

lines.speaker: Kavita
lines.native: شام جو دعوت ٿيندي — تون به ضرور اچ.
lines.roman: shāma jo daʿvata thīndī — tūṃ bi zarūr achu.
lines.en: In the evening there'll be a dinner — you come too.

lines.speaker: Sanam
lines.en: I'll definitely come! What shall I bring?

lines.speaker: Kavita
lines.native: ڪجهه به نه. رڳو بک کڻي اچ!
lines.roman: kujhu bi na. raɠo bukha khaṇī achu!

lines.speaker: Sanam
lines.native: ها ها! ۽ تون واپس ممبئي ڪڏهن ويندين؟
lines.roman: hā hā! ai tūṃ vāpas mumbaī kaɗahiṃ vendīṃ?
lines.en: Ha ha! And when will you go back to Mumbai?

lines.speaker: Kavita
lines.native: مهيني کان پوءِ. پر مان ايندڙ سال وري اچڻ چاهيان ٿي.
lines.roman: mahīne khāṃ poi. para māṃ endaṛa sāla varī achaṇu chāhyāṃ thī.
lines.en: After a month. But I want to come again next year.

culture: **Cheti Chand** marks the birth of **Jhulelal** (also called Uderolal or Zinda Pir), the saint of the Indus revered by Hindu Sindhis and honoured at shared shrines by Muslims too. Celebrations include processions, devotional songs ('ayo lal, jhulelal!') and the **bahrāṇo** (بهراڻو) — an offering of a lamp, sweets and fruit carried to the river or sea. Muslims in Sindh celebrate the two Eids and the ʿurs (death anniversaries) of Sufi saints, such as Lal Shahbaz Qalandar at Sehwan and Shah Abdul Latif at Bhit Shah, which draw hundreds of thousands of pilgrims of all backgrounds.
